findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy Outturn 25-26 covering report Council
findings.headline: Capital programme shows £5.3m underspend with £300k reclassified and major slippage
findings.detail: The capital programme recorded an in-year underspend of £5.299m, but after slippage (carry-forward spending) and accelerated projects, this narrowed to £0.210m net. Critically, the council notes this £0.210m net figure is not a true underspend because £0.300m was reclassified to other budget headings, indicating accounting adjustments not captured in the surface figures.
findings.matters: Large underspends followed by material reclassifications suggest either delayed capital delivery, scope changes, or accounting adjustments that obscure the true capital position and complicate forecasting.
findings.figures: £5.299m in-year underspend; £0.210m net underspend; £0.300m reclassified elsewhere
findings.quote: It should be noted the £0.210m is not a true underspend as £0.300m has had to be reclassified and accounted for elsewhere.

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy Outturn 25-26 covering report Council
findings.headline: Investment property rental arrears worsening with targeted collection intervention planned
findings.detail: The council reports an increase in bad debt on property rents and has specifically allocated additional resource in 2026/27 to improve collection rates on its investment property portfolio. This suggests underlying collection issues that require remedial action.
findings.matters: Rising property rent arrears indicate either weakening tenant quality or collection inefficiency; lenders monitor council asset performance, and uncollected rental income reduces both stated returns and financial resilience.
findings.figures: Increase in outstanding bad debt for property rents; additional resource allocated in 2026/27
findings.quote: There has been an increase in outstanding bad debt for property rents. Additional resource has been allocated in 2026/27 to assist in improving collection rates in investment property.

findings.paper_title: Acceptance of a full Funded Budget Increase in 2026 2027 and utilisation of the Crisis Resilience Fund
findings.headline: All grant funding must be spent by 31 March 2029 or returned to DWP; council has built 9% contingency due to demand forecasting uncertainty
findings.detail: The grant agreement requires all funding to be completely spent by the end of year 3 (31 March 2029) or forfeited. The council has allocated £123,208 as contingency within the £500,000 crisis payments line to account for uncertainty in how many people will apply under the new criteria.
findings.matters: Creates operational pressure to commit funds; if take-up is lower than forecast, contingency cannot be retained; if higher, council cannot expand provision
findings.figures: £123,208 contingency (9% of crisis payments allocation); all funding must be spent by 31 March 2029
findings.quote: It is difficult to estimate how many people will apply under the new criteria for a crisis payment. Therefore, a contingency would be prudent.

findings.paper_title: Acceptance of a full Funded Budget Increase in 2026 2027 and utilisation of the Crisis Resilience Fund
findings.headline: Council faces redundancy and pension strain liabilities when crisis resilience fund staffing contracts end on 31 March 2029
findings.detail: The council is using £126,000 to extend fixed-term staff contracts through 31 March 2029. When these contracts end, redundancy and early pension release will trigger costs payable from the council's own budget into the pension fund, creating an unfunded liability unless future funding is secured.
findings.matters: Creates a crystallized liability post-2029; pension strain can be material and unpredictable depending on employee ages and service records
findings.figures: £126,000 allocated for staff costs through 31 March 2029
findings.quote: Employees made redundant, depending on age and length of service may be entitled to a redundancy payment and early release of pension benefits which may incur a pension strain payable by the Council into the pension fund.

findings.paper_title: Acceptance of a full Funded Budget Increase in 2026 2027 and utilisation of the Crisis Resilience Fund
findings.headline: Fuel oil support and Discretionary Housing Payment allocations beyond year 1 are not yet confirmed
findings.detail: The paper states that fuel oil support (£27,725) is only confirmed for 2026/27, and Discretionary Housing Payment funding for 2028/29 has not been confirmed at all. While base funding for 2027/28-2028/29 is confirmed at £1,771,250 annually, this represents an £85k reduction from 2026/27 and likely reflects the missing fuel oil and unconfirmed DHP components.
findings.matters: Uncertainty about component renewals creates risk of forced service reduction or budget rebalancing if these elements are not continued
findings.figures: £27,725 for fuel oil (2026/27 only); £1,771,250 for 2027/28 and 2028/29 (vs £1,706,183 revenue for 2026/27); DHP funding amount TBD
findings.quote: this may change as there has been no confirmation of any further fuel oil support after year 1 (2026/27). The amount for 2028/2029 will also include the funding for the Discretionary Housing Payments (DHP) which has not been confirmed yet.

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy 2025-26 June 2026 Council
findings.headline: Investment property income has declined with managed workshops operating at only 50% occupancy
findings.detail: The Council's investment property returns have fallen, with the key concern being workshop occupancy at 50% despite active marketing efforts. This represents a reduction in non-tax revenue at a time when other income sources (licensing, crematorium) are also declining.
findings.matters: Declining commercial property returns reduce the council's ability to self-fund services and weaken non-tax revenue resilience; sustained low occupancy may indicate depressed local commercial conditions affecting broader tax base and business rates.
findings.figures: Investment property income variance £54k adverse; managed workshops occupancy 50%; council previously identified investment property income as one of 'key income areas' that has declined during 2025/26
findings.quote: Managed workshops only at 50% occupancy. Marketing underway.

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy 2025-26 June 2026 Council
findings.headline: Council is forecasting to draw on reserves in 2026/27 and 2027/28 to fund revenue deficits despite Fair Funding Review gains
findings.detail: The financial strategy notes the Council will 'use reserves set aside from the underspends and additional income...to fund the shortfalls in 2026/27 and 2027/28' while investing in new corporate priorities. This means even with the Fair Funding Review benefiting Preston (CSP up 7.64% versus 0.57% for comparable councils), the underlying budget still requires reserve drawdowns.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdowns to fund ongoing services (rather than one-off items) indicate underlying revenue pressure and sustainability risk if Fair Funding assumptions change or if planned corporate investment does not generate expected returns.
findings.figures: General Fund balance £16.719m (up from £15.824m); planned reserve use in 2026/27 and 2027/28; CSP up 7.64% in 2026/27 versus only 0.57% average for other district councils
findings.quote: The Council is using reserves set aside from the underspends and additional income, and from the grant funding which must be recognised in the year of receipt, to fund the shortfalls in 2026/27 and 2027/28 while the Council invests in staff capacity and in the new Corporate Priorities.

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy 2025-26 June 2026 Council
findings.headline: External audit costs have increased significantly due to delays in providing timely property valuations
findings.detail: The paper identifies rising audit costs as a key variance area and attributes this specifically to 'issues with providing timely audit evidence in relation to the Council's property and their valuations.' Significant investment is being committed in 2026/27 budget to resolve these governance issues.
findings.matters: Control weaknesses in property valuation and audit evidence create risk that financial position could be misstated; audit delays also create uncertainty about year-end positions and may delay external confirmation of financial standing.
findings.figures: External audit fees variance £92k adverse in 2025/26; 'significant investment has been included in the budget and the financial forecast approved at Budget Council in March 2026 to address the issues'
findings.quote: An area of increased costs has been the Council's external audit costs, and this has been due to issues with providing timely audit evidence in relation to the Council's property and their valuations.

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy 2025-26 June 2026 Council
findings.headline: Bad debt provision has increased significantly, particularly for unpaid Council Tax and investment property ground lease payments
findings.detail: The paper notes an increase in outstanding debts across multiple areas, with particular concern for investment property and Council Tax arrears. The Council has identified this as requiring additional targeted resource in 2026/27 to recover debts and support residents in financial hardship.
findings.matters: Rising bad debt provision indicates deteriorating collection risk and suggests cost-of-living pressures are impacting residents' ability to pay; if arrears continue to grow, this will reduce future revenue and may require further provision increases.
findings.figures: Council Tax deficit of £0.205m accumulated as at 31 March 2026 driven by bad debt provision increases; 'increased pro active action to be undertaken to tackle arrears'
findings.quote: The Council has seen an increase in outstanding debts especially outstanding property/ground lease payments and additional resource has been allocated in 2026/27 to assist in improving collection rates in investment property.

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy 2025-26 June 2026 Council
findings.headline: Council Tax collection rate has fallen to 90.7%, the lowest in five years, with explicit acknowledgement as 'One of the key financial risk areas'
findings.detail: The Council's own assessment identifies collection rates as a principal risk area due to in-year collection rates being low. The decline is driven by significant new house building in North West Preston requiring additional staff resource to process changes and direct debits, compounded by experienced staff turnover and retirements that have reduced collection capacity.
findings.matters: Declining collection rates directly reduce cash available for debt servicing and revenue spending; combined with increasing bad debts, this signals deteriorating collection performance that could persist if staffing issues are not resolved.
findings.figures: 90.7% (2025/26) versus 90.8% (2024/25) and 90.8% (2023/24); accumulated Council Tax deficit £0.205m (Council's share £0.031m); Council Tax collection rate lowest since 2021/22 (90.3%)
findings.quote: One of the key financial risk areas for the Council is current collection rates for Council tax. The collection rates are being closely monitored by the Council due to the in-year collection rates being low.

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy Outturn 25-26 covering report
findings.headline: Capital programme had to reclassify £0.300m, obscuring the true outturn position
findings.detail: The capital outturn shows a £0.210m underspend after slippage, but this masks the fact that £0.300m had to be reclassified and accounted for elsewhere. The reason for the reclassification is not explained.
findings.matters: Unexplained reclassifications of significant capital spending suggest either misclassification, delayed delivery, or capital schemes not proceeding as planned. It makes the true capital position harder to assess.
findings.figures: £0.210m net underspend; £0.300m reclassification
findings.quote: It should be noted the £0.210m is not a true underspend as £0.300m has had to be reclassified and accounted for elsewhere.

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy Outturn 25-26 covering report
findings.headline: Property rent bad debts increased; council allocating additional resources to improve collection in 2026/27
findings.detail: Outstanding bad debt has increased for property rents on investment property. The council is responding by allocating additional resources in 2026/27 to improve collection. This indicates deterioration in collection performance on a revenue stream the council depends on.
findings.matters: Deteriorating rent collection affects cash flow and revenue reliability. It signals either that tenants are struggling or that the investment property portfolio is performing poorly.
findings.figures: Increase in bad debt provision for property rents; specific quantum not disclosed
findings.quote: There has been an increase in outstanding bad debt for property rents. Additional resource has been allocated in 2026/27 to assist in improving collection rates in investment property.

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy Outturn 25-26 covering report
findings.headline: Council's going concern depends on Parliament passing the Structural Changes Order for local government reorganisation
findings.detail: The accounts are being prepared on a going concern basis conditional on Parliament passing the Structural Changes Order for a new unitary council. This creates material uncertainty about Preston's continued existence as a legal entity in its current form, which is fundamental risk for lenders considering the authority's long-term viability and borrowing capacity.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council will continue to exist as a borrowing entity. Reorganisation could change liabilities, assets, tax base, and the identity of the entity they have lent to.
findings.figures: N/A
findings.quote: The annual accounts and outturn position are required to be produced on the going concern basis until Parliament pass the Structural Changes Order for a new unitary council in line with Local Government Reorganisation.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Opinion Report 25-26
findings.headline: Internal Audit has identified key areas of governance where current arrangements could be strengthened, requiring action through the Annual Governance Statement Action Plan.
findings.detail: The council's governance framework received a Reasonable assurance rating. Internal Audit has identified specific areas where current governance arrangements could be strengthened, with the AGS Action Plan containing actions to address these gaps.
findings.matters: Identified governance weaknesses indicate gaps in the council's management and control framework; governance quality is a key factor in assessing credit risk and management competence.
findings.figures: Overall Governance assurance rating: Reasonable
findings.quote: The work of Internal Audit has identified some key areas of governance whereby the current arrangements could be strengthened. The Annual Governance Statement (AGS) Action Plan contains actions to address these areas.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Opinion Report 25-26
findings.headline: Management is implementing audit corrective actions below target rate due to departmental resource constraints, with improvement dependent on budget growth.
findings.detail: Internal Audit reports that agreed management actions from audit findings are being implemented slower than target. Delays are attributed to departmental resource constraints and external factors like software updates. The report hopes improvement will accelerate 'due to the growth items agreed in the budget,' indicating the council is betting on additional budget resources to clear the backlog.
findings.matters: If identified control weaknesses are not being fixed promptly due to resource constraints, those weaknesses persist and accumulate, increasing financial and governance risk.
findings.figures: No specific percentage provided for implementation rate; described as 'below target' but 'improving'
findings.quote: It has been noted that some agreed actions are taking longer to implement with the agreed date extended due to the departments resource issues and external factors, such as software or process updates.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Opinion Report 25-26
findings.headline: Control assurance ratings have deteriorated materially year-on-year, with Substantial ratings falling from 66% to 36% and Limited ratings rising from 5% to 14%.
findings.detail: Preston's internal audit assurance ratings show a significant decline. Substantial assurance (a sound system of controls operating effectively) dropped from 66% to 36%, while Limited assurance (significant gaps requiring improvement) rose from 5% to 14%. This shift towards weaker ratings indicates the control environment is deteriorating.
findings.matters: A material deterioration in control ratings across multiple council systems is a significant risk signal for lenders assessing the council's financial governance and management quality.
findings.quote: The table below shows a percentage comparison of the various levels of assurance for 2025/26 compared with the previous two years.

findings.paper_title: Preston City Council 25-26_Audit Plan - Final
findings.headline: Prior year value-for-money weaknesses only partially addressed; improvement recommendations continuing
findings.detail: The audit plan notes that prior year VFM weaknesses have been only partially addressed, with improvement recommendations from the 2024/25 audit continuing to be followed up. However, the 2025/26 risk assessment has not identified any new significant weakness areas.
findings.matters: Incomplete resolution of audit weaknesses can indicate governance or management implementation gaps, though the absence of new identified weaknesses provides some assurance the council may have stabilised.
findings.figures: 11 prior year audit recommendations made in 2024/25
findings.quote: No new risks of significant weakness reported as one prior year weakness had been fully addressed and the other weakness partially addressed; improvement recommendations made

findings.paper_title: Preston City Council 25-26_Audit Plan - Final
findings.headline: £28.1 million impairment of Animate Development in 2024/25 marked as non-recurring
findings.detail: The audit plan identifies a £28.1 million impairment of the Animate Development that occurred in 2024/25 and was excluded when calculating normalised expenditure for materiality purposes. This represents a substantial loss on a capital investment, though the plan does not explain the cause or whether further losses are anticipated.
findings.matters: A £28.1m impairment signals a significant failed or troubled capital project and raises questions about investment governance, cost control, and whether the council faces further exposure on this or similar schemes.
findings.figures: £28.1 million impairment in 2024/25
findings.quote: We identified the £28.1 million impairment of the Animate Development in 2024/25 as a transaction that should be excluded when determining normalised gross expenditure.

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy Budget Proposals 2026-27 Council March 2026 FINAL
findings.headline: Council is proposing £500k annual discretionary spending on Guild 2032 reserve while drawing down general reserves to fund corporate priorities
findings.detail: The budget proposals include an additional £500k per annum contribution to the Guild 2032 reserve for 2026/27, 2027/28, and 2028/29 (a cultural/legacy project). This is being added while the council is simultaneously drawing £2.5m from general reserves over the same period to fund corporate priorities, signalling a choice to prioritise legacy spending even under reserve-draw conditions.
findings.matters: The decision to fund discretionary cultural spending while drawing down contingency reserves raises questions about prioritisation and the council's risk appetite. It suggests confidence in the forecast, but reduces flexibility if pressures emerge.
findings.quote: For the 2026/27 budget setting process, Cabinet are proposing an additional contribution to the Guild 2032 Reserve of £500k per annum in 2026/27, 2027/28 and 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy Budget Proposals 2026-27 Council March 2026 FINAL
findings.headline: Pension contribution rate reduction of 9.5% is a one-off windfall from the 2025 triennial review, not a structural gain
findings.detail: The Lancashire Local Government Pension Scheme triennial valuation shows the fund at 135% funding, allowing employers' contribution rate to fall from 12.8% to 3.3%. This generates approximately £1.9m annual savings for the council but is specific to this valuation cycle and will be reviewed again in three years. It is not a permanent structural improvement in the council's financial base.
findings.matters: While the savings are real and material, they are temporary and dependent on the fund's valuation at the next review. The council cannot rely on this saving persisting long-term, and rates could move in either direction.
findings.figures: £1.9m per annum, 9.5% reduction in contribution rate from 12.8% to 3.3%
findings.quote: The Pension Fund relating to Preston City Council has been assessed as being funded at 135%, meaning the assets within the fund are greater than the future pension liabilities that the fund... a 9.5% reduction to the Employers Pension Contribution rate. This means that the Councils employee costs will reduce by approximately £1.9m per annum over the triennial review period.

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy Budget Proposals 2026-27 Council March 2026 FINAL
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation uncertainty: council is setting aside £1m and forecasting a 'favourable position' contingent on a Structural Change Order passing Parliament by 2028/29
findings.detail: The council has set aside £1m in earmarked reserves for likely transitional costs of LGR and is forecasting 'no savings requirement from 2028/29' explicitly 'which would be the year of transfer into a new unitary if the Structural Change Order is passed in Parliament.' The forecast depends on this structural change happening; if it does not, budget pressures may extend beyond 2028/29.
findings.matters: The financial forecast is contingent on a structural change that is not yet certain. If the Structural Change Order is not passed, the council's budget position from 2028/29 onwards would need to be reassessed, creating refinancing risk and operational uncertainty.
findings.figures: £1m set aside for LGR transitional costs
findings.quote: In the Mid Year Financial Strategy update in October 2025, Members approved a set aside of £1m into Earmarked Reserves to provide for the likely transitional costs of local government reorganisation... favourable position showing no savings requirement from 2028/29 which would be the year of transfer into a new unitary if the Structural Change Order is passed in Parliament.

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy Budget Proposals 2026-27 Council March 2026 FINAL
findings.headline: New Homes Bonus of £2.136m is being withdrawn from 2026/27 onwards, rolled into Fair Funding with no separate grant
findings.detail: The council received £2.136m of New Homes Bonus in 2025/26. From 2026/27 onwards, this is rolled into the fair funding settlement as a one-off transition, meaning no separate NHB income thereafter. While the Fair Funding Review has increased Core Spending Power by 7.64% overall, the Baseline Funding Level has fallen by 7.68%, creating a complex revenue picture.
findings.matters: Loss of a predictable income stream, even if offset by other grants, reduces revenue certainty and flexibility. The complexity of the Fair Funding transition makes future income forecasting harder.
findings.figures: £2.136m NHB in 2025/26, nil from 2026/27; Baseline Funding Level down 7.68% in 2026/27 to £7.0m
findings.quote: The Council received £2.136m of New Homes Bonus in 2025/26... there will be no separate NHB grant from 2026/27 onwards... The Council's Baseline Funding Level has fallen under the Fair Funding 2.0 allocations... by 7.68% in 2026/27 to £7.0m

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy Budget Proposals 2026-27 Council March 2026 FINAL
findings.headline: General Fund reserves are being drawn down by £2.5m cumulatively over 2026–2028 to fund corporate priorities
findings.detail: The forecast shows the council drawing £1.190m in 2026/27 and £1.364m in 2027/28 from reserves to fund its new corporate priorities, with recovery only from 2028/29 onwards. Starting balance is £15.825m (end 2024/25), falling to £13.118m by 2028/29. While the council maintains this above its £13m prudent minimum, the two-year decline signals intentional use of reserves to manage budget pressures.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdown to fund operating priorities rather than one-off events reduces the council's buffer against unexpected costs or income shortfalls, and signals that revenue budget is insufficient to cover all planned spending.
findings.quote: The Cabinet budget proposals for 2026/27 include use of a proportion of the reserves in 2026/27 and 2027/28 to fund its new Corporate Priorities.

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy Budget Proposals 2026-27 Council March 2026 FINAL
findings.headline: Food waste and Renters Rights Act are adding £895k annual budget pressure with no dedicated funding
findings.detail: The Local Government Finance Settlement requires food waste collection (deadline April 2026) to be funded from the Fair Funding settlement at £755k additional cost. The Renters' Rights Act 2025, effective 1 May 2026, adds around £140k per annum in regulatory responsibilities. Both are unfunded mandates within the settlement, creating persistent budget pressure.
findings.matters: Unfunded regulatory mandates reduce financial flexibility and absorb budget capacity that could otherwise support core services, signalling increasing pressure on council finances from central government requirements.
findings.figures: £755k food waste, £140k Renters Rights Act
findings.quote: the food waste collection service must be met from the new Fair Funding settlement and this has added a budget pressure of £755k to the financial forecast... a budget growth item of around £140k per annum has been included in these budget proposals.

findings.paper_title: Preston City Council Audit Findings Report 2024-25 DRAFT 120226v2
findings.headline: Audit delayed due to missing Animate Development valuation evidence
findings.detail: The completion of the audit was significantly delayed because the Council did not commission a valuation of the Animate Development when it became operational in November 2024. A valuation was not finalized until February 2026, well after the year-end of 31 March 2025.
findings.matters: Delayed audit completion and provision of audit evidence affects the timing and reliability of financial reporting, extending the period before accounts are certified.
findings.figures: Audit period October 2025 – February 2026; Animate became operational November 2024; valuation finalized February 2026
findings.quote: The completion of the audit was delayed as the Council did not commission a valuation of the Animate Development when it became operational in November 2024. A valuation was finalised in February 2026 and resultant amendments to the financial statements actioned with further details set out at page 18.

findings.paper_title: Preston City Council Audit Findings Report 2024-25 DRAFT 120226v2
findings.headline: Investment property valuations increased by £7.7m, driven primarily by agricultural assets
findings.detail: All investment properties were revalued during the year, with a total increase in fair value of £7.7m to £52.685m (from £45.350m in prior year), mainly as a consequence of increases in the value of agricultural investment properties. The Council engaged specialist external valuers for agricultural assets.
findings.matters: A 17% year-on-year increase in investment property values is significant and may indicate concentration risk in agricultural holdings or reflects broader market movements affecting loan security positions.
findings.figures: Fair value increase of £7.7m; investment property value now £52.685m; prior year £45.350m
findings.quote: For investment properties there has been an increase in fair value of £7.7m to £52.685m (PY £45.350m), mainly as a consequence of increases in the value of Agricultural Investment properties.

findings.paper_title: Preston City Council Audit Findings Report 2024-25 DRAFT 120226v2
findings.headline: Multiple asset valuation errors and control weaknesses identified in year-end assessment process
findings.detail: Management's assessment of assets over £500k not revalued during the year identified a net cumulative overstatement of £40k, which was amended. Additionally, investment property valuations contained a £405k error between valuation report and financial statements for two assets. The auditor's independent assessment suggested a potential £1.13m understatement for assets not subject to full revaluation. Multiple individual asset assessments showed changes exceeding the materiality threshold of £104k.
findings.matters: Systematic errors in asset valuation processes, failures to properly assess non-revalued assets, and reliance on cumulative offsetting rather than individual transaction review indicate weak internal controls over financial reporting.
findings.figures: £40k cumulative overstatement; £405k investment property error; potential £1.13m understatement for non-revalued assets; £104k materiality threshold
findings.quote: An assessment of assets not subject to revaluation with a previous value over £500k was completed by the valuer and indicated a net cumulative overstatement of £40k. Management have amended the draft financial statements. We noted that a number of the individual asset assessments indicated a valuation increase or decrease in excess of our triviality level of £104k.

findings.paper_title: Preston City Council Audit Findings Report 2024-25 DRAFT 120226v2
findings.headline: Unexpected long-term absence of key valuation staff caused delays and asset valuation re-work
findings.detail: The Council faced operational challenges in its valuation process during 2024/25 including unexpected long-term absence of a key staff member and loss of a small number of valuations requiring re-performance. The replacement valuation process was completed after draft financial statements were prepared, with a £235k difference between original and revised valuations.
findings.matters: Loss of critical finance staff and resulting control failures in asset valuation represent operational and succession risk that affects financial reporting reliability.
findings.figures: £235k difference between original and revised valuations; multiple re-performed valuations required
findings.quote: The Council faced several further challenges to complete an appropriate valuation programme in 2024/25 caused in part by the unexpected long-term absence of a key member of staff involved in the valuation process, and the loss of a small number of valuations necessitating the re-performance of those valuations.

findings.paper_title: Preston City Council Audit Findings Report 2024-25 DRAFT 120226v2
findings.headline: Revenue accrual of £774k not recorded for 2024/25 income received in 2025/26
findings.detail: Audit identified that the Council did not accrue for income of £774k that was earned in 2024/25 but received in the following year. Management completed further work to confirm no similar errors existed. The financial statements were amended to correct this cut-off error.
findings.matters: Year-end accrual errors indicate control weaknesses in the revenue recognition and close process that a lender would assess as a sign of financial reporting risk.
findings.figures: £774k unaccrued income
findings.quote: Our audit work in this area identified that the Council did not accrue for income of £774k applicable to 2024/25 received in early 2025/26. Management completed further work to confirm that there were not similar errors, and we evaluated that assessment and extended our own procedures. Management have amended the financial statements to correct this error.

findings.paper_title: Preston City Council Audit Findings Report 2024-25 DRAFT 120226v2
findings.headline: Animate Development valuation downward adjustment of £29.199 million made after audit period
findings.detail: The Animate Development became operational in November 2024 but was initially recorded on the balance sheet at accumulated cost without proper valuation. The Council delayed commissioning a valuation until February 2026, after the audit year-end, when CBRE completed an assessment resulting in a major downward adjustment. This delayed valuation significantly impacted the audit process and balance sheet accuracy.
findings.matters: A £29.199m overstatement of a major capital project indicates serious failures in asset management and project governance that would materially affect lending decisions.
findings.figures: Downward valuation of £29.199 million; asset became operational November 2024; valuation completed February 2026
findings.quote: The key issue from our valuation testing related to the Animate Development which became operational in November 2024 and was brought onto the Balance Sheet at accumulated cost. Eventually, the Council commissioned CBRE to complete a valuation of the Animate Development using an appropriate asset classification and valuation basis. The valuation resulted in a downward valuation of £29.199 million and the financial statements have been amended.

findings.paper_title: Preston City Council Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Capital Programme slippage of £1.5m due to schemes awaiting approval, indicating delayed project commencement
findings.detail: The Council delivered 86.7% of the £36.2m revised Capital Programme in 2024/25. Of the slippage observed, £1.5m relates to schemes awaiting approval where necessary authorisations were not obtained in time for schemes to commence as planned.
findings.matters: Delays in capital project approvals can lead to inefficient deployment of resources and extended project timelines; the Council needs to improve approval processes.
findings.figures: £36.2m capital programme; 86.7% delivery rate; £1.5m slippage from approval delays
findings.quote: Capital Programme Slippage - £1.5m of slippage observed in the Capital Programme relates to schemes awaiting approval, where approvals have not been obtained in time for the scheme to commence as planned.

findings.paper_title: Preston City Council Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Data breaches increased significantly from 26 to 41 in the year due to new IT system implementation
findings.detail: The Council experienced 41 data breaches in 2024/25, up from 26 in the prior year. This increase is attributed to implementation of a new IT system requiring testing and embedding. All breaches were handled in-house, deemed low risk by the Council, and did not require escalation to the Information Commissioner's Office.
findings.matters: Rising data breaches indicate information security controls are not yet effective during system transitions; while currently low-risk, this suggests greater monitoring is needed.
findings.figures: 41 data breaches (2024/25) vs 26 (prior year); no escalations to ICO
findings.quote: It does identify that 41 data breaches occurred in year, an increase from 26 in the prior year. This is a result of the implementation of a new IT system, requiring testing and embedding. The breaches were dealt with 'in-house', deemed low risk by the Council and did not require further escalation to the Information Commissioners Office (ICO).

findings.paper_title: Preston City Council Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Harris Project contractor insolvency resulted in £359k net cost impact to the Council
findings.detail: A major external contractor became insolvent during the Harris Project delivery. The Council incurred a net cost impact of £359k after using project contingency, successful legal negotiations, and additional National Lottery funding. The project completed in September 2025 but highlighted weaknesses in external project management arrangements.
findings.matters: Project delivery failures and contractor insolvencies create cost overruns and delays; this incident demonstrates control weaknesses in contractor management and due diligence on complex projects.
findings.figures: £359k net cost impact; project contingency used; additional National Lottery funding obtained
findings.quote: The net cost impact of the previous contractor going into administration on the Council is £359k, which has been limited by existing project contingency, successful negotiations lead by the Council's lawyers and additional National lottery Funding.

findings.paper_title: Preston City Council Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Internal Audit completion rate 74% vs 82% target and management response rate to recommendations only 61% vs 78% target
findings.detail: Internal Audit completed only 74% of the planned audit programme (target 82%) with three audits deferred due to resource constraints. Of actions agreed with Internal Audit across all reviews, only 61% were implemented by management by their target dates (target 78%), though there is evidence of improvement over the year.
findings.matters: Low completion rates for internal controls audits and slow implementation of recommendations increase the risk that control weaknesses go undetected and unaddressed.
findings.figures: 74% of audit plan completed (target 82%); 61% of actions implemented (target 78%); 3 audits deferred
findings.quote: 61% of actions agreed with Internal Audit, across all reviews, were implemented by management. This is below the target of 78%. Although this is below target, there has been evidence of an improvement over the year and ongoing work with management to address outstanding actions. In addition, there was some slippage in the delivery of the audit programme by Internal Audit themselves - 74% of the plan was completed against a target of 82%.

findings.paper_title: Preston City Council Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Audit delays due to inability to obtain timely valuations for land and buildings, with stricter backstop deadlines approaching
findings.detail: The Council continues to experience delays in completing audit work because it cannot obtain valuations and supporting evidence for land and buildings in time. With the backstop deadline for accounts audit moving forward to December 2026 and November 2027, the auditor warns that if this cannot be resolved, they may need to qualify their opinion.
findings.matters: Qualified audit opinions or audit delays signal control weaknesses and create uncertainty for lenders about the reliability of financial statements; this is a recurring issue from prior years.
findings.figures: Backstop deadline moving forward to December 2026 (year ending 31 March 2026) and November 2027 (year ending 31 March 2027)
findings.quote: With the back stop deadline for the audit of the Council's accounts coming forward to December for year ending 31 March 2026 and November for year ending 31 March 2027, it is imperative that the Council get this aspect of the supporting information for the financial statements under control. If work can not be completed in time for the back stop dates we will need to qualify our opinion in this area.

findings.paper_title: Preston City Council Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Council has invested £250k in a community bank with £1m approved in principle, capital at risk and not yet diversified
findings.detail: The Council purchased £250k in shares in a newly established community bank to support small businesses in obtaining finance. The bank is in early stages, has not yet secured its banking licence, and has no other investors. Members approved up to £1m total investment in principle, creating exposure to a venture not yet trading.
findings.matters: This represents a new, concentrated financial risk to the Council where capital may be lost before the venture generates returns; diversification of risk depends on other investors joining, which has not yet occurred.
findings.figures: £250k invested; £1m approved in principle; first branches expected end 2026
findings.quote: The Council has invested in a community bank with the aim of providing finance to small businesses, to boost the local economy. The bank is in the early stages of set-up and the Council investment represents 'seed money' to support the bank in gaining its banking licence and further investors.

findings.paper_title: Preston City Council Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Council plans to use £0.783m of reserves over the medium term instead of developing savings plans
findings.detail: Preston's MTFP to 2028/29 forecasts contributions to reserves in 2024/25 and 2025/26 of £3.814m, followed by a call on reserves in the following 3 years of £4.97m. The auditor notes the Council is relying on reserves to bridge budget gaps rather than identifying savings, which will reduce the General Fund Reserve from 73% to 39% of net expenditure by 2028/29.
findings.matters: Continuous depletion of reserves at this rate (34% reduction over 5 years) is unsustainable; reserves are a finite resource needed to protect against unanticipated financial pressures and are a key measure of financial resilience for lenders.
findings.figures: £0.783m net use of reserves; reserves reducing from 73% to 39% of net expenditure; 34% reduction over 5 years
findings.quote: Continually reducing the General Fund Reserve at this rate would not be sustainable (34% reduction over 5 years, would suggest that in approximately 10 years the Reserve would be depleted if the same pace continued).

findings.paper_title: Report to Council Mid Year Treasury
findings.headline: Council reserves £440k for potential loss of government's pooled investment accounting override after 2029
findings.detail: The council has created a £440k reserve against the possibility that the government's temporary statutory override on pooled investment fund accounting will not be extended past 1 April 2029. The override allows councils to defer recognition of gains and losses; expiry without replacement would trigger accounting adjustments.
findings.matters: This signals genuine uncertainty about government policy affecting council finances. If the override lapses, the council faces potential accounting charges on £14m of externally managed investments, which could impact reported financial position and balance sheet strength.
findings.figures: £440k reserve; externally managed investments £14m; override assumed to expire 1 April 2029
findings.quote: On the assumption that when published regulations follow this policy announcement, the statutory override will be extended up until 1 April 2029 for investments already in place before 1 April 2024. The Council has set up a reserve of £440k to mitigate the impact of the override not being extended past 2029.

findings.paper_title: Report to Council Mid Year Treasury
findings.headline: Capital programme forecast cut by 19% with named projects deferred into later years
findings.detail: The approved capital expenditure forecast has been revised down from £45.8m to £37.1m, a reduction of £8.7m. The deferral affects specific named projects including Amounderness House and Levelling Up park and cycle link projects. The paper does not explain the reasons for the rephasing, leaving the council's ability to deliver these schemes unclear.
findings.matters: A material reduction in a capital plan may signal affordability tightness, project delivery problems, or changed priorities. For a lender, this raises questions about the council's confidence in its capital investment plans and its ability to regenerate town centres as planned.
findings.figures: Original capital expenditure £45.8m; revised to £37.1m (£8.7m deferral); Capital Financing Requirement down from £65.6m to £59.9m
findings.quote: There has been a rephasing of capital expenditure into later years in the Capital Programme. The rephasing relates to projects including Amounderness House, Levelling Up park and cycle link projects.

findings.paper_title: Council October 2025 Mid Year Financial Strategy Update 2025.26 with app
findings.headline: Local government reorganisation creating transition costs and forward planning uncertainty
findings.detail: Lancashire authorities must submit reorganisation proposals to government by 28 November 2025. Preston has set aside £1m in earmarked reserves for transitional costs, plus additional staffing to manage the LGR process. The outcome — whether Lancashire moves to 2, 3, 4 or 5 unitary authorities — is unknown. This creates uncertainty for the council's forward planning and adds costs to the 2025/26 budget.
findings.matters: Major structural reorganisation creates 12+ months of uncertainty over the council's future size, financing, and service boundaries. Lenders care about the stability and predictability of a borrower's revenue base.
findings.figures: £1m set aside to earmarked reserves for transitional costs. Deadline for Lancashire submission: 28 November 2025.
findings.quote: Members are being asked to approve a set aside of £1m into Earmarked Reserves to provide for the likely transitional costs of local government reorganisation... Meetings are set up on 26th November 2025 for Members to consider the LGR submission. The deadline for the Lancashire submission to Government is 28th November 2025.

findings.paper_title: Council October 2025 Mid Year Financial Strategy Update 2025.26 with app
findings.headline: Guild Hall asset requires major investment; RAAC in roof cost not yet quantified
findings.detail: The council's major cultural asset, the Guild Hall, contains RAAC (Reinforced Autoclaved Aerated Concrete) in the roof of the Charter Theatre and Grand Hall. Specialists are still investigating the condition and remediation requirements. The cost and timeline for repairs is not yet known. This represents an unquantified future liability.
findings.matters: Councils with major unquantified asset liabilities face unexpected calls on reserves or borrowing. The scale of work required and timing is unknown.
findings.figures: No figures quantified yet. Noted only as a major asset with significant costs and RAAC presence requiring specialist investigation.
findings.quote: The Guild Hall is a major asset which incurs significant costs. RAAC is present in the roof of the Charter Theatre and the Grand Hall, however specialists are still investigating.

findings.paper_title: Council October 2025 Mid Year Financial Strategy Update 2025.26 with app
findings.headline: New Homes Bonus income stream ending, removing recurring £2.136m
findings.detail: Government has confirmed that the £2.136m one-off allocation in 2025/26 is the final New Homes Bonus payment. This recurring income stream is ending. From 2026/27 onwards the council assumes this funding will be replaced through the Fair Funding Review's broader funding formula, but this is not yet confirmed.
findings.matters: Material loss of non-council-tax income dependent on a formula change that is not yet finalized. Lenders assess council resilience partly through income diversity.
findings.figures: £2.136m (2025/26, final allocation). Previously retained £2.043m from City Deal agreement; this now ends.
findings.quote: The allocation for 2025/26 is a one-year only payment of £2.136m. The Government have indicated 2025/26 will be the final allocation.

news_drafts.headline: Capital programme shows £5.3m underspend with £300k reclassified and major slippage
news_drafts.lead: Large underspends followed by material reclassifications suggest either delayed capital delivery, scope changes, or accounting adjustments that obscure the true capital position and complicate forecasting.

news_drafts.lead: Rising property rent arrears indicate either weakening tenant quality or collection inefficiency; lenders monitor council asset performance, and uncollected rental income reduces both stated returns and financial resilience.
